clinicalScope: Acute seizures in children presenting to low‑resource paediatric wards in East Africa, including both provoked (febrile, metabolic, infectious, toxic) and unprovoked epileptic events.
title: Paediatric Seizures
subject: Paediatrics
summary: A seizure is a brief, abnormal burst of brain activity that can cause jerking movements, loss of awareness or strange behaviour. In African children it is often triggered by fever, malaria, meningitis or low blood sugar, and rapid assessment can save lives.

sections.p: A seizure is a transient disturbance of cerebral neuronal activity producing motor, sensory, autonomic or behavioural changes. In sub‑Saharan Africa, up to 10 % of children will experience at least one seizure before age 5, with higher rates in malaria‑endemic zones.
b: Unprovoked (epileptic) seizures arise from an intrinsic brain disorder.
Provoked seizures have an identifiable trigger such as fever, infection, metabolic derangement or toxin.
Status epilepticus (SE) is a seizure lasting ≥5 min or recurrent seizures without full recovery.
Mortality is highest in SE, especially when associated with severe malaria or meningitis.

sections.h: Causes and risk factors, most likely first
sections.p: In low‑resource settings the hierarchy of causes reflects local disease burden.
b: Febrile illness (malaria, bacterial meningitis, pneumonia) – most common trigger in 6 mo‑5 yr.
Acute metabolic disturbances – hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia.
Neurocysticercosis and tuberculoma – focal seizures in older children.
Toxins – herbal preparations, organophosphates, quinine overdose.
Pre‑existing epilepsy – often secondary to perinatal injury, CNS infection or trauma.

sections.p: Seizures result from an imbalance between excitatory (glutamate) and inhibitory (GABA) neurotransmission, leading to hypersynchronous neuronal firing.
b: Fever lowers seizure threshold by increasing neuronal metabolism and cytokine release.
Hypoglycaemia deprives neurons of ATP, impairing ion pumps and causing depolarisation.
Inflammatory cytokines in meningitis increase blood‑brain barrier permeability, facilitating excitotoxicity.
Neurocysticercosis lesions act as a focus for abnormal electrical discharge.

sections.p: Presentation varies with seizure type and underlying trigger.
b: Generalised tonic‑clonic: sudden loss of consciousness, stiffening, then rhythmic jerks, followed by post‑ictal drowsiness.
Focal motor: unilateral jerking, eye deviation, may evolve to bilateral involvement.
Febrile seizure: occurs within 24 h of fever onset, lasts <15 min, no prior epilepsy.
Status epilepticus: continuous convulsion or repeated seizures without regaining baseline.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and rapid exam guide urgent management.
b: Onset: time, duration, precipitating fever, trauma, ingestion, recent illness.
Previous seizures or known epilepsy? Antiepileptic drug (AED) adherence?
Vaccination status – meningitis risk.
Examination: airway patency, breathing, oxygen saturation, glucose finger‑stick, fever, focal neurological signs, meningeal signs.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic seizures must be excluded, especially when treatment differs.
b: Syncope with myoclonic jerks – brief, rapid recovery, no post‑ictal confusion.
Movement disorders (e.g., dystonia) – sustained abnormal postures, no loss of consciousness.
Psychogenic non‑epileptic seizures – prolonged, variable pattern, often triggered by stress.
Hypoxic events – apnea, cyanosis, bradycardia preceding movement.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Prioritise tests that are available and will change immediate care.

t.b: Is hypoglycaemia the trigger? <2.2 mmol/L confirms need for dextrose.

t.a: Full blood count & malaria rapid test
t.b: Is malaria or bacterial infection present? Positive malaria test → start antimalarial; leukocytosis with neutrophilia → consider bacterial meningitis.
Identify metabolic precipitants. Na <125 mmol/L or Ca <2.0 mmol/L requires correction.
Detect bacterial or cryptococcal meningitis. CSF WBC >100 cells/µL with neutrophils → bacterial meningitis.
Distinguish epileptic from non‑epileptic activity; epileptiform discharges support epilepsy diagnosis.

b: Stage 1: Brief seizure (<5 min), fully recovers – observe, treat trigger.
Stage 2: Recurrent seizures without full recovery – initiate second‑line AED (phenobarbital).
Stage 3: Status epilepticus – airway protection, continuous benzodiazepine infusion, consider ICU transfer.
Red flag: respiratory compromise, hypoxia (SpO₂ <90 %), persistent post‑ictal coma.

sections.p: Local factors can obscure diagnosis or worsen outcome.
b: Concurrent severe malaria → cerebral malaria may mimic seizures.
HIV infection – opportunistic CNS infections increase seizure risk.
Traditional herbal remedies – may contain neurotoxic alkaloids.
Limited access to EEG or neuro‑imaging → reliance on clinical judgement.

sections.p: Stabilise, treat trigger, then consider anticonvulsants.
b: 1. Airway, breathing, circulation – place child laterally, give oxygen if SpO₂ <90 %.
2. Check glucose; give 2 mL/kg 10 % dextrose IV if <2.2 mmol/L.
3. Treat obvious infection – antimalarial (artesunate) or ceftriaxone for meningitis per national protocol.
6. Avoid drugs that lower seizure threshold (e.g., high‑dose quinine, bupropion).
7. Monitor vitals, glucose, seizure frequency; treat complications (aspiration, hypoxia).
Status epilepticus – risk of neuronal injury, respiratory failure.
Aspiration pneumonia – especially after tonic‑clonic phase; watch for fever, crackles.
Traumatic injury – tongue bite, facial bruising, fractures from falls.
Neuro‑cognitive decline – repeated uncontrolled seizures over months.

sections.p: Certain paediatric sub‑populations need tailored care.
b: Neonates – consider hypoxic‑ischemic encephalopathy, inborn errors of metabolism; give phenobarbital as first‑line.
Children with sickle cell disease – higher risk of stroke‑related seizures; urgent neuro‑imaging if available.
HIV‑positive children – screen for cryptococcal meningitis, TB meningitis.
Malnourished children – electrolyte disturbances are common precipitants.

sections.p: Outcome depends on cause, seizure control and prevention of recurrence.
b: First febrile seizure with normal exam → excellent prognosis, no long‑term AED needed.
Recurrent unprovoked seizures → start maintenance AED (phenobarbital or carbamazepine) after acute phase.
Prevent malaria with insecticide‑treated nets, prophylaxis where indicated.
Educate caregivers on fever management, safe storage of chemicals, and prompt medical review for any new seizure.

sections.p: Be aware of false‑negative or non‑specific findings.
b: Normal CSF in early cerebral malaria – still treat malaria if clinical picture fits.
Glucose may be normal after a brief hypoglycaemic episode; repeat if suspicion remains.
EEG may be normal after a single seizure; do not rule out epilepsy solely on this.
Rapid malaria test can miss low‑parasitaemia; consider microscopy if high suspicion.

whenToSeekHelp: Seizure lasting >5 minutes or multiple seizures without recovery
Signs of meningitis (neck stiffness, bulging fontanelle) or severe malaria (coma, severe anaemia)

faq.q: Are all seizures in children caused by epilepsy?
faq.a: No – most are provoked by fever, infection or metabolic problems; only a minority are due to an underlying epilepsy.

faq.q: Why is phenobarbital preferred over newer AEDs in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: It is inexpensive, widely available, has a long half‑life and can be given orally, making it practical where monitoring is limited.

faq.q: Can a child with a single febrile seizure develop epilepsy later?
faq.a: The risk is only slightly higher than the general population; most children do not develop epilepsy.

exam: A 3‑year‑old with malaria presents with a 6‑minute generalized convulsion – what is your immediate management and why? — Secure airway, give oxygen, check glucose, treat hypoglycaemia, give IV diazepam, start antimalarial; these steps address life‑threatening complications and the underlying cause.

How does febrile status epilepticus differ from a simple febrile seizure in terms of prognosis? — Status epilepticus carries higher risk of neuronal injury and mortality; simple febrile seizures are self‑limited and have excellent prognosis.

A child has a focal seizure with a history of recent head trauma – which investigation is most urgent and what finding would change management? — Urgent non‑contrast CT (if available) to look for intracranial bleed; detection of hematoma would prompt neurosurgical referral.
Why should high‑dose quinine be avoided in a child with seizures? — Quinine can lower seizure threshold and precipitate convulsions, worsening the clinical picture.
Explain the pathophysiological link between hypoglycaemia and seizures. — Low glucose impairs ATP‑dependent ion pumps, leading to neuronal depolarisation and hyper‑excitability, triggering seizures.

In a child with known epilepsy who presents with breakthrough seizures, what are the three most common reversible causes to assess? — Non‑adherence to medication, infection/fever, metabolic disturbance (e.g., hypoglycaemia, electrolyte imbalance).

What clinical sign helps differentiate a true seizure from a syncope with myoclonic jerks? — Post‑ictal confusion and a prolonged recovery period are typical of seizures; syncope recovers within seconds without confusion.

When is it appropriate to start maintenance phenobarbital after an acute seizure? — After the acute phase when the child has had ≥2 unprovoked seizures or a single seizure with high risk of recurrence (e.g., structural lesion).

A child with HIV presents with seizures; CSF is normal. Which condition must still be considered and why? — Cerebral toxoplasmosis or cryptococcal meningitis can have normal early CSF; empirical treatment may be needed based on clinical suspicion.
